params.textField: When vomiting occurs due to damage to the cerebral cortex or due to emotions is best treated with the *Benzodiazepines* like *Alprazolam*. The pathway from the inner ear to the vomiting centre uses two different neurotransmitters, Histamine 1 and Acetylcholine. As such, if there are spasms in the GIT, the best medication is one of the *Anticholinergics* like *Hyoscine*. If there are no spasms, it is treated with one of the *Antihistamines* that break into the blood brain barrier like *Diphenhydramine*. Importantly however, none of these three types of medication will have much of a therapeutic effect if the vomiting is caused by damage to the GIT or from the toxic effects of drugs. Those medications are discussed in the next lesson.

params.textField: You are taking your three friends for a boat trip and you have just three medications in your first aid kit. Joel has bad allergies but does not get sea sick. He is the skipper, and should be given *Loratadine, an antihistamine that stays out in the periphery*. Alma has had some digestive problems today with some overactivity and she is susceptible to getting motion sickness. She should get *Hyoscine, the anticholinergic agent*. Vivaan gets very bad motion sickness but he is not the skipper, and intends to just ‘lay back’. He should get *Diphenhydramine, an antihistamine that breaks into the blood brain barrier*. This case is discussed in the video lesson if you have any questions about it.

params.textField: The neurotransmitter Serotonin 3, abbreviated 5HT3 is used to relay messages from the GIT cells to the neuron that carries the information to the vomiting centre, in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, and in the pathway from the chemoreceptor trigger zone to the vomiting centre. This means that *Ondansetron* and other *5HT3 receptor antagonists* are the most effective medications that we have for chemotherapy induced vomiting. *since that neurotransmitter is not used in many places in the body or brain, it is relatively free of side effects*. Another neurotransmitter that is used in two of those pathways is the dopamine 2 neurotransmitter. Therefore *dopamine 2 antagonists* like *prochlorperazine* are useful for vomiting that originates in the GIT and to some extent, the chemoreceptor trigger zone. *since that neurotransmitter is used throughout the brain, it is associated with many side effects*
